newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: Bond yields moved almost 20 basis points lower in quiet Monday trade, helped by short-covering ahead of Wednesday's budget and buying triggered by three new eurorand issues, dealers said.
At the local close, the key R150 was pegged at a 14.83 percent yield compared with 15.02 percent on Friday.
Buyers initially drew their impetus from a strong showing by U.S. Treasury bonds on Friday.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. bond moved to a 6.81 percent yield from 6.88 percent on Thursday in the wake of a wage inflation report which tempered fears of a Fed tightening in the short-term.

The demand pulled local bond yields down to around the 14.95 percent level by noon, before three new eurorand issues -- a 150 million rand World Bank five-year bond and two EBRD zero coupon bonds -- triggered further buying in the afternoon.
Dealers said the market was also buoyed by short-covering as the market geared up for Wednesday's budget presentation.
"There are some good expectations about the budget, although people may be expecting a bit too much," a trader said.
"The market has largely discounted a positive budget and people feel that barring any unexpected surprises, there shouldn't be much reaction to the budget," another trader said.
Key among the market's expectations are that Finance Minister Trevor Manuel will announce that government is on track to meet its 4.0 percent deficit target in 1997/98.
Market players are also expecting no increase in value added tax, a slight adjustment in tax brackets as well as the usual increase in "sin taxes".
A partial relaxation of exchange controls, specifically the issue of a bond for blocked rand funds as well as allowing local residents to hold foreign exchange accounts offshore, is also expected.

Until Finance Minister Trevor Manuel unveils his budget at 1215 GMT on Wednesday, dealers said the market was expected to move sideways from its current levels. A breach of the 14.82 percent level on the downside, however, could herald further gains, a dealer added.
Volumes on the day were expected to match those of Friday's, which the Bond Exchange pegged at a paltry 2.7 billion rand from 34.65 billion rand on Thursday -- settlement day.
The exchange also said foreigners were net sellers of 10.37 million rand's worth of South African bonds on Friday after selling 39.87 million rand on Thursday.
The rand also ended stronger on the day, helped in part by the firmer bond market which dealers said prompted exporters to offload dollars, albeit in small amounts, into the market.
At the finish, the rand was quoted at 4.4460/4490 against the dollar from 4.4625/4655 previously.
"We saw some local exporters come through and knock it below 4.45 but it has been on extremely low turnover and almost no interbank interest," a trader said.
The currency was expected to move in a 4.42 to 4.47 range ahead of Wednesday, they said.
Against the crosses, the rand was last quoted at 7.1036/1110 against sterling from 7.1419/1624 previously and at 0.3835/3840 marks from 0.3846/3850 marks on Friday.
The Reserve Bank indicated the money market shortage at a record high of 11.680 billion rand on Saturday from 11.645 billion rand on Friday.

The Reserve Bank's money and capital market assistant general manager Roelf du Plooy said the reason for the continued high shortage was the fact that commercial banks were assuming the central bank's role of providing forward cover to South African businesses.

He expected the shortage to remain high at least until the end of this week. "As long as banks keep more dollars on their portfolios we can expect the shortage to remain high. I don't see an immediate reduction in the shortage in the short-term," he said.

The high shortage had no impact on short-term rates as three-month deposit rates held steady at between 16.50 to 16.70 percent and the 90-day BA rate held Thursday's 15.90 percent offered to 16.10 percent bid range.
-- Paul Richardson, Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
